title: Local Mean Solar Clock
intro: Local mean solar time (LMT) uses the average daily motion of the Sun and the observer's longitude rather than a political time zone.
structure: The display uses conventional 24-hour fields followed by LMT. Longitude changes the reading by four ordinary minutes for each degree east or west. Mean solar noon is 12:00 in this model; it is not necessarily the instant the actual Sun crosses the meridian.
example: At 12:00 UTC, longitude 15 degrees east gives 13:00 LMT, while longitude 30 degrees west gives 10:00 LMT. Longitude zero gives 12:00 LMT. A time-zone or daylight-saving change does not change these results.
history: Before widespread adoption of standard time zones, towns often used local mean time. The offset depended on their meridian rather than a national time standard.
model: The provider adds longitude × 240 seconds to the positive UTC day phase, wraps the result modulo 86400 seconds and floors to the displayed whole second or minute. The following visible boundary is scheduled with upward millisecond rounding. The longitude input must be finite and within the valid geographic range.
limits: This is a mean solar approximation using UTC as a surrogate for Earth rotation time; the interface supplies neither DUT1 nor historical observatory corrections. It is not apparent sundial time. Longitude, not latitude, determines the result; a compatible consumer must supply valid location metadata rather than silently defaulting to Greenwich.
